## What the model says

In an m-alternative forced-choice task (m-AFC) one of `m` alternatives holds the signal, and the observer
picks the alternative with the strongest evidence ([DeCarlo, 2012](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmp.2012.02.004)).
The signal alternative draws its evidence from a distribution located at `d`, each of the `m` − 1 distractors
from the same distribution located at 0, all with scale 1 (for the normal distribution, SD 1). `dist` names
the shape, as on the [yes/no page](sdt_yn.qmd): `normal`, `logistic`, or one of the two skewed Gumbel
distributions. The response is correct when the signal's evidence exceeds that of every distractor. With $f$
the density and $F$ the cumulative distribution function of that distribution at location 0 and scale 1,

$$
P(\text{correct}) = \int f(x - d)\, F(x)^{m - 1}\, dx .
$$

Read from the inside: $f(x - d)$ is the density of the signal's evidence at $x$, and $F(x)^{m - 1}$ the chance
that all `m` − 1 distractors fall below $x$; the integral adds this up over every $x$. `d` is the only
parameter: m-AFC has no criterion and no response bias. Under normal noise at `m` = 2 the integral is
$\Phi(d/\sqrt{2})$, with $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function; both Gumbel distributions also give
closed forms. For normal noise at `m` > 2 and for logistic noise bmm sums the integral over fixed points
(numerical quadrature), and this page uses the same points, so its numbers are bmm's. A row of data holds the
number of correct responses out of `n_trials` trials, which is binomial with probability P(correct). `d` is on
the scale of the `d` of the [yes/no model](sdt_yn.qmd): at `m` = 2 under normal noise, P(correct) equals the
area under the yes/no ROC curve of the same `d`.

## The task

One trial presents `m` alternatives, intervals, locations or items, and one of them holds the signal: in
forced-choice recognition, the studied item among `m` − 1 new ones. The participant picks one. bmm fits counts:
each row of the data holds `n_correct` correct responses out of `n_trials`. The number of alternatives `m` is
the task setting that enters the likelihood: it fixes how many distractors, `m` − 1, the signal has to beat.
`sdt_mafc()` takes it as a number, or as the name of a data column when it varies between rows.

## Explore

In the task panel, the tiles show one trial with the current `m`; the orange tile holds the signal, which the
observer does not know. Next to them are the evidence densities: the signal alternative's (orange), one
distractor's (dashed grey), and the density of the strongest of the `m` − 1 distractors (solid grey), which is
what the signal has to beat. The strongest of several draws tends to be high, so that density sits to the right
of a single distractor's and moves further right as `m` grows, and accuracy falls. Raising `d` moves the signal
density to the right. The panel "P(correct) by d, at this m" shows accuracy for every `d` at the current `m`:
chance, 1/`m`, at `d` = 0, and below chance for negative `d`, where the signal sits below the distractors.

The `d` slider spans bmm's default prior, normal(1, 1) (mean 1, SD 1), from mean − 3 SD to mean + 3 SD (−2 to 4),
and starts at the prior mean, 1 (dashed line). `m` runs from 2 to 10.

## Across task settings

`m` is the design variable of this model: with `d` fixed, accuracy falls as `m` grows, because the signal has
to beat the strongest of more distractors. How fast it falls depends on the evidence distribution. At one `m`,
each distribution can reproduce any accuracy, because each has its own `d` to adjust, so data from a single `m`
cannot tell the distributions apart. In the panel "P(correct) across m", each of the other three distributions
gets the `d` that gives the current accuracy at the current `m`; the legend lists these values. They differ
because the distributions differ in spread and in shape: `gumbel_min` and `gumbel_max` have the same spread, and
at `m` = 2 the same `d` gives both the same accuracy, but they are skewed in opposite directions, and from `m` = 3
on they need different values of `d` for one accuracy (except at `d` = 0, chance). The dotted lines meet at the
circle and separate at other values of `m`; how far depends on `d` and `m` (the sentence below gives the
numbers), and where they stay close they can lie on top of each other. Several values of `m` in one data set,
passed to `sdt_mafc()` as a column, are what lets the data decide between the distributions.

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="sdtmafc-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="sdtmafc-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/sdt_mafc.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `sdt_mafc()` names the data columns, the number of alternatives and the
evidence distribution, `dsdt_mafc()` returns the log likelihood of a count of correct responses, and `bmm()`
estimates `d` from data; `my_data` stands for your own data, and fitting runs Stan through brms. See the
[signal detection article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_sdt.html) and the reference pages for
[`sdt_mafc()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/sdt_mafc.html) and
[`dsdt_mafc()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/sdt_mafc_dist.html).
